# Implement block: Unlocking Checkout Steps (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Unlocking Checkout Steps" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

The confirming steps of a checkout on white: the title "Confirm", three step dots (a green check, a black "2" with "DELIVERY DETAILS", a grey "3") and the order's card with "Order 12329", "$19.11", "Placed on 3 June 2022" and a large square button, grey with a down arrow. A light grey drawer under the card asks one thing at a time: "SELECT AN OPTION" with Delivery and Pickup, where the suggested one sits in a grey pill that turns black when tapped; that unfolds "DELIVERY BY", a strip of hours whose middle pill turns black the same way; and that unfolds "DELIVERY TO" with "Home" and a teal "Change", at which the card's button turns green and its arrow turns to the right. Confirm folds the drawer away while the two black picks fly up to the card's right side, the option landing as plain words and the hour as a pill; the price greys, the card grows to show the address over a street map on which a teal route draws itself, the third dot takes over and a green "Done" appears. Done grows into a green sheet that takes the whole screen, on which a drawn parcel with a check badge, "Checkout successful!" and a black "Return to Dashboard" scale up; returning puts the form back as it started.

**Motion.** A tapped option or hour fills from grey to black in 180 ms, dips to 0.9 in 90 ms and bounces back on a spring (damping 8, stiffness 320, mass 0.8); the option pill slides between the two options on a spring (damping 17, stiffness 240). 180 ms after a choice the next section unfolds on a spring (damping 17, stiffness 150, a little overshoot): the drawer grows by the section's height (138 pt, then 136 pt, under the first 118 pt) while its content fades in from 20% to 90% of the way. With the hour chosen the button goes from grey to green and its arrow from down to right in 380 ms (ease-out cubic). The arrows of the strip step the hour and a tap on a neighbouring hour brings it to the middle and chooses it; labels cross-fade (180 ms in, 120 ms out). Confirm runs one spring from 0 to 1 (damping 18, stiffness 130): the drawer's height goes to nothing and it fades between 20% and 70%; the option pill travels from the drawer to 26 pt inside the card's right edge, 32 pt from its top, shrinking from 122 × 58 to 86 × 24 while its black fades out by 80% and its label turns dark; the hour pill travels to 68 pt from the top, 82 pt wide, going from 58 to 48 pt high; the card grows from 160 pt to the summary's height, the button and the rule fade out in the first 40%, the address row and map fade in from 45%, the second dot becomes a check and its name closes up as the third dot turns black and its name opens; Done fades in from 60% and rises 18 pt; 350 ms later the route draws over 700 ms (ease-in-out cubic). The second dot goes back to the choices along the same spring. Done runs a 520 ms clock (ease-in-out cubic): the green sheet takes the screen's width in the first 40% and its height from 8% to 100% while a copy of the label grows to 2.6 times and fades between 15% and 70%; from 70% the drawing, title and button fade in and scale up from 0.7 on a spring (damping 13, stiffness 150), and 200 ms after the flood the check draws in 320 ms. "Return to Dashboard" resets the form behind the green and fades it out in 360 ms. Buttons give a light haptic. The self-playing demo loops every 10 s with no haptics, each press shown for 150 ms first: Delivery at 0.8 s, the hour at 2 s, Confirm at 3.6 s, Done at 5.6 s and "Return to Dashboard" at 8.2 s; a touch takes over and 3 s after the last one the form goes back to its start (in 300 ms) and the loop begins again. Under reduced motion sections open in 160 ms and the summary in 200 ms without springs, nothing bounces or rises, and the success screen fades in without scaling. On Android 26–27, the card shadow uses a bounded Gaussian coverage approximation.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [UnlockingCheckoutStepsDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Forms/UnlockingCheckoutSteps/UnlockingCheckoutStepsDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [CheckoutArt.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Forms/UnlockingCheckoutSteps/CheckoutArt.swift)
- [UnlockingCheckoutSteps.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Forms/UnlockingCheckoutSteps/UnlockingCheckoutSteps.swift)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
